title: Beneficiaries and inherited accounts
teaches: Why beneficiary forms override wills, the choices a surviving spouse has with an IRA, the ten-year rule for other heirs, and how to withdraw an inherited IRA with the least tax

blocks.text: Retirement accounts, life insurance and accounts marked payable or transfer on death pass by their beneficiary forms, not by the will. A will written last year that leaves everything to the children doesn't touch a 401(k) whose form, filled in at a first job, names a parent who has since died or an ex-spouse.

For many households these forms control most of the money. Each account needs a primary beneficiary, who inherits first, and a contingent one, who inherits if the primary has died, checked after every marriage, divorce, birth and death. Washington law revokes an ex-spouse's designation automatically on divorce for most assets, but not for employer plans governed by federal law, as the US Supreme Court decided in a case from Washington.[^egelhoff] A 401(k) also needs the spouse's written consent to name anyone else.

Taxable brokerage and bank accounts can carry a transfer-on-death designation too, which names who receives them, and Washington allows a transfer-on-death deed for a house. With all of them, little is left to pass through **probate**, the court process that carries out a will.
A spouse who inherits an IRA can roll it into their own IRA and treat it as theirs from then on, with required withdrawals based on their own age. That is usually best for an older survivor.

A younger survivor may do better leaving it as an inherited IRA for a while. Withdrawals from an inherited IRA carry no 10 percent penalty before 59 and a half. A widow of 50 who needs to live on the account can draw from it freely; rolled into her own IRA, the same withdrawals would be penalised. They can roll it into their own IRA later, once past 59 and a half.

Since 2020, most other heirs must empty an inherited IRA or 401(k) by the end of the tenth year after the death. If the owner had already begun required withdrawals, the heir must also take a withdrawal each year in between; if not, they can take any amounts in any years, as long as the account is empty by year ten.[^edb]

The freedom over timing is worth a lot. An heir earning $150,000 who takes a $1 million IRA in one lump pays most of it at 35 and 37 percent. Spread evenly over ten years, the same money is taxed mostly at 24 and 32 percent, about a quarter less tax in all. An heir with no salary in those years does better still: a tenth a year then costs about $131,700, under 40 percent of the lump sum's $350,800. One who retires partway through can move most of the withdrawals into the years after.

blocks.text: An inherited Roth follows the same ten years but is tax-free, so the best plan there is usually the opposite: leave it untouched to grow until the tenth year, then take it all.

Naming a trust as beneficiary lets the owner control what happens to the money: for a young heir, a spendthrift, or someone receiving disability benefits. The trust must be drafted to qualify as a see-through trust,[^see-through] or, if the owner died before their required withdrawals began, the account may have to be emptied within five years, a stricter rule than the ten. A trust that holds on to the money it withdraws, rather than paying it out to the heir, pays tax itself, and trusts have compressed brackets: the top 37 percent rate starts at about $16,000 of income. So these trusts are written with care.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Beneficiary forms, not the will, decide where retirement accounts go: name a contingent and review them after every change in the family.
A surviving spouse can roll an IRA into their own, or keep it inherited to draw without penalty before 59 and a half.
Most other heirs must empty an inherited account within ten years.
Spreading withdrawals over the ten years saves tax, and moving them into years with no salary can halve it.
Inherited Roths are best left to grow until the tenth year.

blocks.caption: Four questions on beneficiaries
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A will leaves everything to the children; the IRA's form names the owner's sister. Who gets the IRA?
items.why: The beneficiary form decides, whatever the will says.

items.ask: A widow of 52 inherits her husband's IRA and needs income from it. What is usually best?
choices: Keep it as an inherited IRA for now
Roll it into her own IRA at once
items.why: Inherited IRA withdrawals have no early penalty; her own IRA's would until 59 and a half.

items.ask: An adult son inherits a traditional IRA from a father who hadn't started required withdrawals. When must it be empty?
choices: By the end of the tenth year after the death
items.why: Most non-spouse heirs follow the ten-year rule.

items.ask: Why is it usually best to leave an inherited Roth untouched until the tenth year?
choices: Its growth is tax-free, so the longer it grows the better
The tenth year has lower rates
items.why: With no tax on withdrawals, there is no reason to take them early.

summary: **Beneficiary forms override wills.** Name a contingent, and review after every family change.
**A spouse can roll over or wait.** An inherited IRA can be drawn without penalty before 59 and a half.
**Other heirs have ten years.** With yearly withdrawals too if the owner had started them.
**Spread the withdrawals.** Low-income years in the ten can halve the tax.
**Let an inherited Roth grow.** Take it at the end of the ten years.
**Trusts need careful drafting.** Or they speed up the withdrawals and pay the top rate.

egelhoff.title: Egelhoff
egelhoff.text: David Egelhoff of Washington died soon after his divorce, with his ex-wife still named on his employer's life insurance and pension. Washington law said the divorce revoked her designation; in 2001 the Supreme Court held that federal pension law overrode the state statute, and she kept the money. The lesson is to change the forms, not rely on the law.

edb.title: Eligible designated beneficiaries
edb.text: Some heirs can still stretch withdrawals over their own life expectancy: a surviving spouse, a minor child of the owner until 21, a disabled or chronically ill heir, and anyone not more than ten years younger than the owner. Final IRS rules issued in 2024 confirmed the yearly withdrawals within the ten years when the owner had started theirs.

see-through.title: See-through trusts
see-through.text: Under IRS rules, a trust itself is not a person, so an IRA left to a plain trust loses the ten-year rule. A see-through trust qualifies because it is valid under state law, becomes irrevocable at death, has identifiable human beneficiaries, and gives the IRA custodian its paperwork on time. The IRS then looks through the trust to the people behind it.
